title: State of the ART: Functional genomics of RNA-binding proteins and their role in artemisinin drug resistance in Plasmodium falciparum
text:
The artemisinin family of drugs are the most effective frontline class of drugs used to treat infections with
Plasmodium falciparum, the deadliest malaria-causing parasite in humans, yet the emergence of artemisinin
resistance threatens disease eradication efforts. Our understanding of the molecular mechanisms implicated in
artemisinin resistance remains incomplete. This project investigates how RNA-binding proteins, important post-
transcriptional regulators of gene expression, support artemisinin resistance in P. falciparum.

title: Protein kinase C and lung carcinogenesis
text:
KRAS mutations represent one of the most frequently recurrent initiating events in lung cancer. We identified
protein kinase C epsilon (PKCe) as an essential player in KRAS- and carcinogen-mediated lung tumor initiation,
and as an important regulator of signaling that promotes lung cancer cell motility and invasion. In this application
we will investigate the molecular basis of the permissive role for PKCe in oncogenic KRAS-mediated lung tumor
development and identify downstream effectors responsible for PKCe-driven lung tumorigenesis and metastatic
phenotypes.

title: Developing and Evaluating a Nature-Based Culturally Grounded Alcohol and Drug Prevention Intervention for American Indian Youth and their Families
text: RESEARCH PROJECT 3: PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT Settler colonialism involved the appropriation of American Indian and Alaska Native (AI/AN) land and harmful federal Indian child removal policies. Consequences include disrupted family relationships and unresolved grief, which often led to coping through alcohol and other substances. Among AI/AN adolescents, historical trauma contributes to risk of alcohol use disorders and sleep disturbances but exposure to nature improves sleep and decreases alcohol and substance misuse in youth. Thus, we use the Indigenous Traditional Ecological Knowledge framework to develop a land-based intervention addressing cultural and spiritual mechanisms be- tween nature and wellbeing. Our nature-based culturally grounded intervention will focus on experiential learning with “fellow relatives” (e.g., animals, plants, water, land), exposure to nature, and cultural lessons delivered by Traditional Knowledge Holders to AI/AN youth and their families. We hypothesize that the intervention will enable wellbeing through healthy coping strategies, which will deter early alcohol use and improve sleep. Led by a team of Indigenous researchers, our study will use community-based participatory research principles and will priori- tize Indigenous knowledge to collaborate with a Tribe in Montana to develop and test the outdoor nature-based culturally grounded intervention using stratified block randomization with controls receiving a version of the in- tervention adapted for indoors. Our Specific Aims are to: 1) Co-develop the nature-based culturally grounded prevention intervention for AI/AN youth (ages 11-14); conduct interviews using an Indigenous research data collection approach, research yarning, with seven to nine Traditional Knowledge Holders to determine the sea- son-based modules using Indigenous Traditional Ecological Knowledge framework; 2) Evaluate the nature- based culturally grounded intervention for implementation effectiveness and refine modules to fit the local con- text; conduct three talking circles with approximately 21 high-risk AI/AN youth and their family members, and intervention implementers to identify facilitators, barriers, and strategies that will support program participation; and 3) Test whether the nature-based culturally grounded intervention decreases prevents or reduces alcohol use and improves sleep, by randomly assigning participants to the nature-based culturally grounded program in nature (n=120; intervention) or a modified version of the nature-based culturally grounded program in a class- room setting (n=120; control). This Research Project provides an important opportunity to understand how na- ture-based culturally grounded programs can address critically important behaviors—alcohol use and sleep— that can have lasting impacts on AI/AN young people’s health outcomes.

title: Genomic and Clinical Mechanisms and Prognostic Implications of Myocardial Lipomatous Metaplasia
text:
Scar within heart tissue has traditionally been seen as the instigator of heart pump dysfunction and electrical
irregularities. My post-doctoral research has revealed that fat infiltration is more critical than scar in facilitating
poor outcomes in heart disease. The proposed study aims to investigate fat infiltration into the heart, using data
from the Penn Medicine Biobank, to develop better treatments and improve patient outcomes.
Project Narrative

title: Discovery of Novel Therapeutics for Inflammation Induced Preterm Birth
text:
Preterm birth is the leading cause of infant morbidity and mortality throughout the world. Intrauterine infection
and/or inflammation is a major trigger of early labor leading to preterm birth. The goal of this project is to identify
novel therapeutic agents to manage infection-induced inflammation leading to preterm labor and protect against
fetal inflammation without adverse side effects to the fetus.

title: Determining the Stoichiometry of Endogenous Voltage-gated Potassium Channels in the Brain
text:
Most ion channels are composed of multiple proteins, known as subunits, that each affect channel physiology,
with the precise combination of subunits varying between different neuronal cell types, tissues, developmental
stages, and diseases. However, due to technological limitations, the composition and subunit arrangement of
most endogenous ion channels (i.e., those in an organism rather than those assembled in a dish) remain a
mystery. We have developed a novel strategy for solving the structures of endogenous ion channels at
resolutions high enough to reveal subunit composition, and will use this methodology to probe the functional
diversity of voltage-gated potassium channels in the mouse brain in health and disease.

title: Preventing Spinal Infection: Ultrasound Triggered Prophylaxis
text:
Postoperative infection is a catastrophic and far too frequent complication (up to 9% incidence) of spinal fusion
surgery, with existing preventative measures being only partially successful. To combat this clinical problem, this
renewal application will produce a novel, biodegradable, US-triggered, antibiotic-release system to locally target
bacteria, and assess it in vitro and in vivo (animals). At the end of this study, we will have created a method for
noninvasive, timed, local delivery of antimicrobials, and made a significant impact on antibiotic prophylaxis and
treatment, especially against bacteria that survive the initial prophylaxis, a major cause of both acute and chronic
infections.

title: Altered Hippocampal Neurogenesis and Cognition via Maneb-mediated Changes in the Thiol Redox Proteome.
text:
Down syndrome, a genetic condition resulting in the triplication of chromosome 21, occurs in 1 in approximately
700 live births in the United States of America. We believe that, due to this genetic condition, Down syndrome
patients are more vulnerable to toxic chemicals in the environment, and that these exposures contribute to the
variability of intellectual disability observed in this patient population. This project is designed to test this
hypothesis.

title: Regulation of pathogen sensing and inflammation by NLR proteins
text:
The negative regulation of inflammation is necessary to prevent an overzealous response. Perturbations in the
balance of an appropriate response, either too aggressive or attenuated, underlie immunopathology,
transformation and chronic metabolic syndrome. Understanding the molecular mechanisms of negative
regulation of inflammation will be necessary for the generation of new strategies to improve health.

title: Cancer Control and Population Sciences (CCPS)
text: CANCER CONTROL AND POPULATION SCIENCES PROGRAM ABSTRACT The Huntsman Cancer Institute (HCI) Cancer Control and Population Sciences (CCPS) Program integrates the broad range of research areas that define the cancer control and populations sciences field as it applies to individuals and families in HCI’s catchment area. These research areas span studies of cancer predisposition genetics and chemoprevention trials in high-risk patients to studies designed to improve risk communication and risk-reducing behaviors for the most prevalent cancers. They also include explorations in health outcomes and research to understand and improve disease and treatment outcomes. CCPS Aims cover three broad areas of population sciences research: cancer genetics, cancer risk reduction, and improving cancer outcomes. These support HCI's overall mission to understand the basis of cancer and to use that knowledge to create and improve cancer treatments and prevention measures. The CCPS specific aims are: 1) to translate cancer predisposition genetics and genomics to the clinic and the population; 2) to develop and implement interventions that reduce cancer risk; and 3) to explore and improve outcomes related to cancer diagnosis, treatment, survivorship, and end-of-life, while simultaneously enhancing value in cancer care. The CCPS Program has 57 members, representing 21 departments and eight schools or colleges, providing a rich environment for team science. Cancer-relevant, peer-reviewed extramural funding in 2018 included 68 projects totaling $9.5M in direct costs. CCPS members direct their research squarely on problems central to cancer, underscored by an exceptional record of cancer funding, with $4.9M (52%) of the Program’s extramural peer-reviewed funding deriving from the National Cancer Institute. Between 2014 and 2018, there were 925 cancer-relevant publications from this highly productive and collaborative Program. Of these publications, 242 (26%) involved intra-programmatic collaborations and 164 (18%) involved inter- programmatic collaborations. The program also makes exceptional contributions to clinical trials, with more than >7,400 accruals to investigator-initiated interventional and observational studies. CCPS Program research has many impacts: 1) genetics and genomics work contributes to understanding cancer from its beginnings; 2) cancer risk and cancer prevention research works to continue reducing cancer incidence in HCI’s catchment area; and 3) the broad portfolio of outcomes studies contributes to improving cancer diagnosis and treatment, while also reducing suffering during recovery from treatment and subsequent survivorship. Products from these Aims are poised to impact cancer incidence and outcomes in HCI’s catchment area and cancer care delivery broadly.

title: COBRE PHASE III:  Center for Neuroplasticity at the University of Puerto Rico
text:
UPR COBRE Center for Neuroplasticity
During Phase 3 the UPR Center for Neuroplasticity will continue to provide a multidisciplinary cadre
of investigators with cutting-edge facilities, scientific capability, and multidisciplinary collaborations for
the treatment of neurodegeneration-related diseases. Our projects are unified by shared thematic
and technical factors toward understanding and treating neurological disorders, including, the
origins of neural and mental health disorders, as well as elucidating the molecular basis for alcohol
neuroadaptation, addiction, and neuroprotection. Our center will become a world-recognized center
for the study of neurodegeneration-related diseases with therapeutic applications.

title: Microscopy Laboratory
text: The Microscopy Core Laboratory Shared Resource (MICROS) provides expert, state-of-the-art, affordable, and cost-effective light, electron, and cryo-electron microscopy imaging to Perlmutter Cancer Center (PCC) members and their collaborators, regardless of their pre-existing expertise. As advanced microscopy and image analysis is central to modern cancer research, MICROS is heavily utilized and essential to all 4 Research Programs, with TIM, CCB, and CGD the heaviest users. Since the 2018 CCSG review, 55 funded grants and 92 peer-reviewed publications used MICROS data. MICROS is directed by Feng-Xia (Alice) Liang, PhD an internationally recognized expert in the field with >30 years of experience in microscopy and >15 years of experience as a shared resource director. Dr. William Rice oversees cryo-EM services and has >20 years of experience and >60 publications. MICROS has nine expert staff members who fully support PCC members with project consultation, experimental design, sample preparation, imaging, data analysis and interpretation, high resolution structure determination, and curated image data for grant applications and publications. During the funding cycle, MICROS expanded and relocated to newly renovated space that houses a centralized light microscopy suite, an adjacent cryo-EM suite, and a nearby electron microscopy suite for state-of-the-art TEM and SEM. The new suites provide updated data networking, new instruments, imaging technology, and advanced imaging services to PCC members, including 2D and 3D imaging and optimized high-throughput and superresolution microscopy. MICROS shares and disseminates technological expertise to drive multidisciplinary collaborations, while ensuring quality control of imaging data, instrumentation, equipment, and data provenance. Like most other shared resouces, MICROS is overseen by the Division for Advanced Research Technologies, has an advisory board of PCC members and other NYU faculty and solicits yearly surveys to assess member needs. The Specific Aims of MICROS are 1) To provide PCC members with cost-efficient, high quality, state-ofthe- art access to, and expertise in, the latest cutting-edge imaging technologies, including optical microscopy, two- and three-dimensional (2D and 3D) electron microscopy, and cryoEM, and evaluate and implement emerging imaging technologies, 2) To provide PCC members with consultation, experimental protocol design, and training in high resolution structure determination, image analysis and interpretation, and image data management, 3) To educate and inform the PCC scientific community about advanced imaging technologies and applications to cancer research through frequent informational advanced microscopy seminars, instrument demos, the weekly PCC Faculty Lunch, and presentations/posters at the PCC Retreat and other institution-wide seminar series.

title: Consortium for food allergy research clinical center CoFar
text:
Novel therapies for food allergies and thorough understanding of the mechanisms associated with food allergy
and tolerance are pressing needs of utmost priority. We will evaluate the safety and efficacy of microbiota
transplantation therapy in teens with peanut allergy and investigate the role of novel biomarkers in predicting the
outcome of peanut oral food challenge or peanut oral immunotherapy. We also will contribute extensively to the
Consortium of Food Allergy Research as a Clinical Research Center through successful implementation,
scientific expertise, and training of the next generation of NIH funded investigators skilled in food allergy.

title: Expanding single-cell and spatial technologies to link clonal genotypeswith phenotypes during cancer evolution
text:
Cancer mutations drive the outgrowth of small populations of cells in normal tissue, years before clinical
diagnosis of cancer, or the outgrowth of cells resistant to therapy. However, how such mutations change cellular
behavior to provide them with a competitive growth advantage over adjacent cells remains poorly understood.
To address this gap in knowledge, we propose to apply and develop novel single-cell sequencing technologies
to study the mechanisms underlying growth advantage in cancer.

title: The Florida Pediatric NCORP renewal application for grant# UG1CA189973 to continue participation in the NCI Community Oncology Research Program.
text: Cancer is the single largest cause of death due to disease in children. While the incidence of childhood cancer is low compared to adults, outcomes measured in terms of life years lost make it a major public health concern. Participation in clinical cooperative groups provides the best chances for improved patient outcomes. This application provides for community site access to those trials that, in conjunction with current COG sites, extend research access to the entire state of Florida, the third most populous state in the country.

title: Project IV - Isolating placental effects of environmental toxicants in fetal development: AI/ML-augmented multi-omic causal discovery and prognostic modeling
text: Project Summary – Project 4 Exposure to per- / poly-fluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), a large class of persistent, pervasive, and physiologically active, environmental contaminants, are a major potential source of adverse pregnancy and child health outcomes. However, the role of the placenta in regulating exposure to and effects of these chemicals is not well studied. Past research has been limited in two major ways: (a) Methods to quantify placental function have been too broad relying on estimates of total gene expression quantified using non- specific references from other tissues; and (b) While it is necessary to study the effects of PFAS in real life human settings, existing statistical methods do not well account for the many potentially unmeasured factors (confounders) that could explain observed PFAS effects. Since gene expression in placenta is vastly different from other adult tissues, this has strongly limited our understanding of which specific PFAS may be harmful and how to mitigate such harms. This project will address these gaps by developing a novel resource based on long-read sequencing (Nanopore platform) technology to better capture the various gene transcripts (at the isoform-level) produced by the placenta (Aim 1.1). Using this resource, we will investigate the relationship of various PFAS to gene expression in an observational cohort (N = 200) while leveraging an AI/ML computational approach to integrate other genomic (epigenomic) data to address unmeasured confounding (Aim 1.2). Further, it will use these findings in a decomposition model to specifically quantify the extent to which different levels of PFAS exposure, in conjunction with variation in placental function, result in varying effects of PFAS across populations (Aim 1.3). Next, it will utilize information about PFASs they appear to have causal effects on placental function to develop clinical prediction models for adverse pregnancy and birth outcomes (Aim 2.1). Specifically, we develop cross-validated ensemble Machine Learning / Deep Learning to fit best predicting models using baseline (pre-pregnancy) and PFAS concentration data and compare performance improvement over traditional models. Next, we will apply this model to an independent cohort with real preconception data to validate its clinical utility (Aim 2.2). Together, we hypothesize that our computational approaches will be able to be better distinguish environmental contaminants that have true causal effects which will be validated through their improvement of risk prediction models. This work sets the stage to apply these approaches to investigating other putatively causal biomarkers in non-experimental data. 1

title: Robust Actin Filament Modeling in Low-Resolution Cryo-ET Images Using Advanced Deep Learning and Algorithmic Techniques
text:
This project aims to develop a novel open-source computational framework to enable precise quantifica-
tion of actin filament morphology from cryo-electron tomography data. By facilitating the discovery of how
structural alterations in actin drive disease mechanisms in cancer and cardiomyopathies, this work ad-
dresses a critical public health challenge. Our integrated approach bridges a fundamental gap between
cellular imaging and pathological insight, providing a foundation for future therapeutic strategies.

title: Antigen specific treatment of AChR myasthenia gravis with an engineered biologic
text: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune orphan disease with an estimated 1.4 million cases worldwide. Current treatments leave patients immunocompromised and highly susceptible to a host of infections and medical complications. This proposal seeks to develop a targeted non-steroidal and non-immunosuppressive MG treatment without the side effects of current immunotherapies.

title: Using Machine Learning for Early Recognition and Personalized Treatment of Acute Kidney Injury
text:
Up to 20% of hospitalized patients develop acute kidney injury, which is associated with increased risk of
readmission, morbidity, and mortality. This project will use advanced machine learning methods and
biomarkers to improve the identification and treatment of patients at risk of acute kidney injury. This project will
result in novel tools and personalized treatment algorithms that can be implemented to improve patient
outcomes.

title: E-Box Accessibility in Myofibroblasts in Pulmonary Fibrosis
text:
Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) is a fatal scarring disease of the lung. We will test the hypothesis that the
myofibroblast program in pulmonary fibrosis is regulated by two parallel and essential events: the accessibility
of E-Box motifs and the expression of E-Box-binding transcription factors including TWIST1.
